title: 6.1 Federal Reserve and Interest Rates
summary: Macro news can sound far away from the chart in front of you.
bodyHtml:
6.1 Federal Reserve and Interest Rates

Why This Matters

Macro news can sound far away from the chart in front of you.

But if you trade products such as EUR/USD, gold, the S&P 500, or Treasury bonds, changes in interest-rate expectations can affect your market quickly.

You do not need an economics degree to use this lesson well.

You only need to understand one core idea:

interest-rate expectations are one of the main forces that shape borrowing costs and asset prices across the financial system

What You Should Understand After This Lesson

By the end of this lesson, you should be able to:

  • explain what the Federal Reserve is trying to do in plain language;
  • describe how rate expectations can affect bonds, the U.S. dollar, stocks, gold, and oil;
  • use the FOMC calendar as a risk-timing tool instead of a prediction tool.

What the Fed Actually Does

The Federal Reserve, or Fed, is the central bank of the United States.

On its monetary policy page, the Fed says its actions and communications are meant to promote:

  • maximum employment;
  • stable prices;
  • moderate long-term interest rates.

For a beginner, the easiest way to think about this is:

the Fed helps set the tone for the cost of borrowing money in the U.S.

That matters globally because U.S. rates influence:

  • bond yields;
  • the value of the U.S. dollar;
  • borrowing conditions for companies and households;
  • the way investors compare risky assets with safer ones.

The Fed is not the only central bank that matters. The same logic also applies to major institutions such as the European Central Bank and the Bank of England. The Fed gets extra attention because the U.S. dollar is so important in global trade and finance.

Three Terms You Need

Term Plain-English meaning Why traders care
Interest-rate decision A choice to raise, lower, or hold the policy rate It can change market expectations quickly
FOMC The Federal Open Market Committee, the Fed group that sets policy This is the meeting traders watch on the calendar
Yield The return investors demand from assets such as bonds Yield moves can spill into currencies, stocks, and gold

(Table alt-text: A three-row table explaining interest-rate decision, FOMC, and yield in simple language for beginners.)

Why Rates Move More Than One Market

Interest rates do not only matter to bond traders.

They can affect several markets at once because they change how investors compare:

  • holding cash;
  • owning bonds;
  • buying stocks;
  • holding assets such as gold that do not pay income;
  • pricing future growth and demand in markets such as oil.

Here is a simple cross-asset view:

Market What higher-rate expectations can often do Why
Bonds Pressure bond prices and lift yields Older fixed payments look less attractive when new rates are higher
U.S. dollar Support the dollar Higher expected U.S. yields can attract capital
Stocks Pressure growth-sensitive shares and indices Higher discount rates and borrowing costs can hurt valuations
Gold Create headwinds for gold Higher yields can raise the opportunity cost of holding a non-income asset
Oil / energy Influence demand expectations and dollar-sensitive pricing Slower-growth fears or a stronger dollar can pressure oil, while easier policy can support demand-sensitive assets

(Table alt-text: A five-row table showing common cross-asset effects of higher rate expectations on bonds, the U.S. dollar, stocks, gold, and oil.)

These are tendencies, not guarantees.

Markets move based on expectations, surprises, positioning, and broader risk mood. A rate hold can still move markets sharply if traders expected a cut. A hike can cause less damage than expected if the market had already priced it in.

The Calendar Matters More Than Prediction

A disciplined beginner does not try to outguess every Fed sentence.

A disciplined beginner asks:

When is the event, and should I reduce risk before it hits?

The Fed says the FOMC holds eight regularly scheduled meetings during the year. As of March 12, 2026, the 2026 FOMC page lists eight scheduled meetings, and the next meeting after this lesson date is March 17-18, 2026.

The statement on a decision day is commonly released at 2:00 p.m. U.S. Eastern Time. Always confirm the official calendar because schedules, statements, and related materials are published there.

One Simple Example

Imagine you trade gold.

It is 1:50 p.m. U.S. Eastern Time on an FOMC day. You see what looks like a breakout and feel tempted to buy immediately.

Now stop and ask:

  1. Is this breakout still worth taking if a major policy statement is due in 10 minutes?
  2. If the statement surprises the market, could gold move sharply before my order fills cleanly?
  3. Am I trading my chart plan, or am I drifting into a news gamble?

The disciplined answer for many beginners is simple:

  • do not open a fresh trade seconds before the announcement;
  • wait for the statement;
  • let the first reaction settle;
  • then study the new structure.

That is not being timid. That is professional timing.

Common Beginner Mistakes

Mistake 1: Thinking Only Bond Traders Need to Care

Rates can affect currencies, stocks, commodities, and volatility.

Mistake 2: Treating the Fed as a Prediction Game

The lesson is about risk awareness, not perfect forecasting.

Mistake 3: Ignoring Time Zones

Always convert event time to your own local time before the session starts.

Mistake 4: Treating Every Reaction as Permanent

The first move after a statement is not always the lasting move.

quizItems.prompt: Which statement best describes the Federal Reserve in this lesson?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It sets the exact price of every asset

choices.label: B
choices.text: It uses monetary policy and communication to pursue maximum employment and stable prices

choices.label: C
choices.text: It only matters to bond traders

correctAnswer.label: B
correctAnswer.text: It uses monetary policy and communication to pursue maximum employment and stable prices

quizItems.explanation: The lesson frames the Fed as a central bank whose policy stance influences financial conditions, not as a direct controller of every market price.

quizItems.prompt: Why can a Fed decision affect more than one market at once?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Because rates can influence yields, the dollar, stock valuations, and the appeal of holding cash or gold

choices.label: B
choices.text: Because every market closes during the statement

choices.label: C
choices.text: Because only U.S. stocks trade on Fed days

choices.label: D
choices.text: Because the Fed controls commodity production

correctAnswer.label: A
correctAnswer.text: Because rates can influence yields, the dollar, stock valuations, and the appeal of holding cash or gold

quizItems.explanation: The lesson teaches cross-asset transmission, not a single-market effect.
quizItems.lessonAnchor: Why rates move more than one market

quizItems.prompt: What is the best beginner use of an FOMC calendar?

choices.label: B
choices.text: Know when conditions may become unstable and avoid poor timing

choices.label: C
choices.text: Ignore it unless you trade bonds

correctAnswer.label: B
correctAnswer.text: Know when conditions may become unstable and avoid poor timing

quizItems.explanation: The calendar is used for risk timing and preparation, not certainty.
